## 1. What you'll build, and why

A compiler that produces correct, fast machine code is still missing something a real toolchain
has: **debuggability**. When you set a breakpoint at line 12 and the debugger stops there — when you
single-step and the source line tracks the program counter — that's **debug info** at work: a
mapping from machine addresses back to source locations. This concept builds the foundational piece,
the **line table**, and threads it through the whole backend, so a `swiftml`-built native binary can
be stepped in `lldb` by source line.

It's the last piece of **M8-core**: the from-scratch ARM64 backend is correct (concept 33),
fast (34), ABI-conformant (35), polished (36) — and now **debuggable**.

- **You implement:** `emit_loc` — emitting a `.loc` source-line directive whenever the line changes.
- **Outcome:** the built object has a real DWARF line table (`dwarfdump` confirms address→line), and
  `lldb` steps the binary by source line.

> **What's a line table?** Compiled code has no idea it came from "line 12" — it's just
> instructions. The **line table** is a side table the compiler emits: a list of (machine address →
> source file, line) rows. The debugger reads it to answer both directions: "the PC is `0x70`, so
> we're at line 5" (for stepping and stack traces) and "the user wants line 5, so set the breakpoint
> at `0x70`." It's the single most important piece of debug info — breakpoints and stepping need
> nothing else.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### Threading a source line end-to-end

![A source line, threaded all the way through: SILGen stamps each SIL value with its statement's line (a `lines : value→line` map on the SIL function); isel emits a `.loc 1 N 0` directive whenever the line changes; `clang -g` assembles those directives into a real DWARF line table (address→line); and `lldb` follows it to set breakpoints by line and step. macOS keeps the DWARF in the `.o` plus a debug map in the executable, so we keep the `.o`.](figs/debuginfo.png)

The line number starts at the front end and has to *survive* every lowering. Here's the chain:

1. **AST → line.** Every statement carries a span with a line number; `Ast.stmt_line` extracts it.
2. **SILGen stamps it.** The builder keeps a `cur_line`, set at the top of each `gen_stmt`. Its
   `emit` — the one place every SIL value is created — records `lines[v] = cur_line`. So *every* SIL
   value remembers the source line of the statement that produced it. The SIL `func` carries this
   `lines : value → line` map alongside `val_ty`.
3. **isel emits `.loc`.** As isel lowers each SIL instruction `(v, …)`, it looks up `lines[v]`. When
   the line *changes* from the last one emitted, it emits an `Arm64.Loc n` — a `.loc 1 n 0`
   directive. Consecutive instructions from the same statement share one `.loc`, so the table is
   compact.
4. **The assembler builds DWARF.** A `.file 1 "src.swift"` names the source; `clang -g` turns the
   stream of `.loc` directives into the DWARF `.debug_line` section — a real line-number program
   mapping each instruction address to its source line.
5. **lldb reads it.** Breakpoint-by-line and single-stepping both consult this table.

The elegance is that the *line table is the easy part* once the line is threaded — `emit_loc` is
three lines. The work is the plumbing (SILGen stamping every value), which is given; you write the
`.loc` emission.

### Why `.loc` directives instead of hand-encoded DWARF

DWARF's line-number program is a tiny bytecode (special opcodes that advance the address and line
by deltas, to compress the table). We *could* hand-encode it — but the assembler already does, from
`.loc` directives. Emitting `.file`/`.loc` and letting `clang -g` build the `.debug_line` section is
exactly how every compiler that targets the GNU/LLVM assembler does it (LLVM's `MCStreamer` emits
`.loc`; the integrated assembler encodes the program). We get a *real, standard* DWARF line table for
the cost of one directive per line. Hand-encoding the line program is the exercise — worth doing once
to see the bytecode, but not the point here.

### The macOS debug-map wrinkle

On Linux, DWARF lives in the executable and you're done. macOS is different: the DWARF stays in the
**object file**, and the linker leaves a **debug map** in the executable (a table of `N_OSO` symbols
pointing at the `.o` files). `lldb` follows the map to the `.o` to read the DWARF; `dsymutil` can
also gather it into a `.dSYM` bundle. The practical consequence for us: `clang -g file.s -o exe`
compiles to a *temporary* `.o`, links, and **deletes** the `.o` — so the executable's debug map
points at nothing and `lldb` finds no line info. The fix is to **keep the `.o`**: assemble to
`<out>.o`, then link it. Now the debug map resolves and `lldb` steps. (Our `dwarfdump` test reads the
`.o`'s line table directly, which is reproducible regardless of the link step.)

### What you can do with it

```bash
$ swiftml8 build square.swift --native -o square      # builds square + square.o (with DWARF)
$ lldb square
(lldb) breakpoint set --file square.swift --line 3
Breakpoint 1: where = square`square + …, address = 0x…
(lldb) run
Process stopped at square.swift:3
   1   func square(_ n: Int) -> Int {
   2     let r = n * n
-> 3     return r
   4   }
(lldb) step
```

The debugger is stepping through *our* register-allocated, peephole-optimized ARM64 — and the source
line tracks it, because every instruction carries the line it came from.

> Oracle: the DWARF spec's "Line Number Program" chapter; LLVM's `.loc`/`.file` MC directives;
> `man dwarfdump`; Apple's debug-map documentation (DWARF-in-`.o` + the linker's `N_OSO` map).

## 3. Build it, step by step

In `isel.ml`, implement `emit_loc vv` (called before lowering each SIL instruction). Given:
`f.Sil.lines` (the `value → line` map filled by SILGen), and `last_line` (the last line emitted):

- look up `Hashtbl.find_opt f.Sil.lines vv`;
- if it's `Some line` with `line > 0` and `line <> !last_line`: set `last_line := line` and
  `emit (Arm64.Loc line)`;
- otherwise do nothing (so consecutive instructions on the same statement share one `.loc`).

The line threading (SILGen stamping, the `lines` map, the `.file` directive, the `-g` build keeping
the `.o`) is given. Reference: `solution/isel.ml`. Run with
`make lab C=phase8-arm64-backend/37-debug-info`.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase8-arm64-backend/37-debug-info
```

cram: the asm has a `.file` and one `.loc` per statement line; the built `.o` has a DWARF line table
whose addresses map to exactly the source lines with code (`dwarfdump --debug-line` shows
`2 3 5 6 7 8`); programs still run and match `swiftc`. alcotest: a `.loc` is emitted for each source
line; adjacent `.loc`s never repeat a line (deduped per statement); SILGen stamps SIL values with
their line; the printed asm contains `.file` and `.loc`.

## 5. Benchmark it

Debug info has no runtime cost — the `.loc` directives and DWARF live in the object file, not the
executed code. The measurable quantity is the *size* of the line table: one row per line change, a
few bytes each after DWARF's delta encoding. Compare the `.o` size with and without `-g`; the line
table is a small, fixed tax for a debuggable binary, which is why production builds ship it (often in
a separate `.dSYM`) by default.

## 6. Exercises

1. **Hand-encode the line program.** Emit the DWARF `.debug_line` section yourself — the header plus
   the line-number program (special opcodes that advance address/line by deltas) — instead of
   `.loc` directives. The right way to *understand* the table you've been generating.
2. **Variable locations (`.debug_info`).** Emit DWARF DIEs for each function and its variables, with
   location expressions (`DW_OP_fbreg` for a frame slot, a register for an allocated value). Now
   `lldb` can `print x`. This is the big next layer.
3. **Column info & is_stmt.** Track columns (not just lines) and mark statement boundaries precisely,
   so the debugger steps statement-by-statement and points at the right sub-expression.
4. **A `.dSYM`.** Run `dsymutil` after the link to gather DWARF into a bundle, so the executable is
   debuggable without keeping the `.o` — the production macOS workflow.
5. **Inlined frames.** When concept 19's inliner splices a callee, emit DWARF inlined-subroutine
   info so `lldb` shows the original call stack even though the call is gone.

## 7. Recap & what's next — M8-core complete

Debug info is a **line table**: a map from machine addresses to source lines. We thread the line from
the AST (SILGen stamps every SIL value), emit a `.loc` when it changes (your `emit_loc`), let
`clang -g` build the DWARF, and keep the `.o` so `lldb` resolves it. The result is a `swiftml`-built
native binary you can step through by source line — the last piece of **M8-core**.

**Milestone M8-core is reached:** the from-scratch ARM64 backend — instruction selection, a
register-allocation ladder, AAPCS64 conformance, peephole polish, and debug info — compiles the
scalar + control-flow + functions corpus correctly (differential vs both the LLVM path and `swiftc`),
fast (graph-colouring ~2.9× over the naive baseline), and debuggable. Two backends now share one
front end.

Next is the **project's final tail**: **38-async-await** (coroutine lowering + a cooperative
executor), **39-actors** (isolation), and **40-macros** (a compile-time expression-macro expander) —
completing the language and the course.

## 8. Appendix — full solution

```ocaml
(* the line table emission (isel), called before lowering each SIL instruction *)
let last_line = ref 0 in
let emit_loc (vv : Sil.value) : unit =
  match Hashtbl.find_opt f.Sil.lines vv with
  | Some line when line > 0 && line <> !last_line -> last_line := line; emit (Arm64.Loc line)
  | _ -> ()
in
... List.iter (fun (vv, i) -> emit_loc vv; sel_instr vv i) (List.rev b.Sil.instrs) ...
```

The given threading: SILGen's `emit` stamps the line, and `gen_stmt` sets it.

```ocaml
let emit (b : builder) (instr : Sil.instr) (ty : Types.ty) : Sil.value =
  let v = b.next_val in
  b.next_val <- v + 1;
  b.cur.Sil.instrs <- (v, instr) :: b.cur.Sil.instrs;
  Hashtbl.replace b.val_ty v ty;
  Hashtbl.replace b.lines v b.cur_line;            (* <- stamp the source line *)
  v

and gen_stmt (b : builder) (s : Ast.stmt) : unit =
  b.cur_line <- Ast.stmt_line s;                   (* <- set it per statement *)
  match s with …
```

And the printer renders `.file`/`.loc`:

```ocaml
if m.source <> "" then Buffer.add_string b (Printf.sprintf "\t.file\t1 %S\n" m.source);
…
| Loc n -> Printf.sprintf "\t.loc\t1 %d 0" n
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — hand-encode the line program
Emit the `.debug_line` section directly: the unit header (version, address/line bases, opcode
lengths), then the program — for each row, a `DW_LNS_advance_pc` / `DW_LNS_advance_line` pair (or a
*special opcode* that does both in one byte when the deltas are small), ending each sequence with
`DW_LNE_end_sequence`. It's the bytecode the assembler was generating from your `.loc`s; writing it
once demystifies the format.

### 2 — variable locations
Emit `.debug_info` DIEs: a `DW_TAG_subprogram` per function, with `DW_TAG_variable` children carrying
a `DW_AT_location`. For a spilled value, the location is `DW_OP_fbreg <offset>` (frame-relative); for
an allocated value, `DW_OP_reg<n>`. The hard part is that an allocated value's location *changes*
over its live range — you'd emit a location *list*. With this, `(lldb) print r` works.

### 3 — column info & is_stmt
Track the column from the span (`span.lo.col`) and pass it as the third `.loc` field; mark the first
instruction of each statement `is_stmt` and others not, so the debugger's "step" lands on statement
boundaries and the source highlight points at the right sub-expression.

### 4 — a .dSYM
After linking, run `dsymutil <out>` to read the debug map + `.o` DWARF and produce `<out>.dSYM`. Now
the executable is debuggable without the loose `.o` — the standard macOS ship format. (`lldb`
auto-loads a `.dSYM` sitting next to the binary.)

### 5 — inlined frames
When the inliner (concept 19) splices a callee, record the original call site and the callee's line
info, and emit `DW_TAG_inlined_subroutine` DIEs with `DW_AT_call_line`. `lldb` then reconstructs the
*logical* call stack — showing `square` in the backtrace even though it was inlined away — which is
why optimized builds remain debuggable.
```
